newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nissan says plans to cut types of car platforms.
newsitem.headline: Nissan says plans to cut types of car platforms.

text.p: Japan's Nissan Motor Co Ltd announced on Tuesday that it will follow its foreign rivals in cutting back on the type of car platforms it uses in a drive to cut costs and boost global competitiveness.

The planned cut in the number of basic car platforms, to be implemented by 2000, was seen as a positive step for the carmaker by investors who pushed up its shares on the Tokyo bourse, but some industry analysts remained sceptical.

"We plan to reduce (the types of platforms) drastically as a way to cut production and development costs but we cannot disclose at this moment how many types we will cut. And we are not yet clear on how much we can reduce costs," a spokesman for the nation's second-biggest automaker told Reuters.
Nissan now has 15 types of platforms used in domestic and overseas production. The platform consists of the chassis and suspension and does not include the engine and transmission.

The economic daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported on Tuesday that Nissan would cut five of the platforms used in its models worldwide by 2000, hoping to save some 300 billion yen ($2.63 billion) in development and production costs a year.
Under the plan, Nissan's popular Sunny compact and Bluebird medium-sized models would share one platform, as would minicars, station wagons and sport-utility vehicles produced in Europe, it said.

The paper said that plan would help rebuild Nissan's sluggish business performance in Europe. In the year to March 1997, Nissan pulled itself out of the red on a group basis for the first time in five years.
The Nissan's announcement comes at a time when foreign rivals such as Volkswagen AG, General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co are struggling to cut the number of their basic platforms.
Ford, for instance, has set up a five-year global product development plan, which calls for the number of basic platforms to drop by 50 percent.
And in April, Mazda Motor said it had agreed with Ford to synchronise car production cycles and share common platforms in a bid to cut costs.

Nissan's announcement helped push up its shares by 10 yen to 817 yen at the Tuesday close of the Tokyo bourse, but some analysts warned that Nissan's move could backfire by making its products featureless and less attractive to consumers.
"It's almost a gamble," said Seiji Sugiura, an analyst of Nomura Securities Co Ltd's research unit.

Even though it will help Nissan cut costs, "it may reduce sales because motor enthusiasts hate (the idea of using the same platform) because they consider the platform a key component of driving performance," Sugiura said. "If platform sharing is done between sedans and sports cars, Nissan may lose clients," he said. ($1=114 yen)
